analytic.title: Utilization-based Schedulability Test of Real-time Systems on Virtual Multiprocessors

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: The number of applications that use virtual systems is growing, and one would like to use this kind of systems also for real-time applications with hard deadlines. Virtual machines with many cores are interesting since the underlying physical infrastructure usually contains many cores.

We consider hard real-time tasks that execute on a virtual machine with m cores. Tasks are scheduled globally on the cores using fixed-priority preemptive scheduling. This means that a task can execute on different virtual cores at different instances in time. In order to avoid Dhall's effect, which may cause task sets with even very low utilization to miss deadlines, we classify tasks into two priority classes, namely heavy and light tasks. Heavy tasks have higher priority than light tasks. For light tasks we use rate monotonic priority assignment. In this paper we propose a utilization-based test that shows if a task set is schedulable or not. If the task set is schedulable the test provides the priority for each task. The input to the test is the task set, the number of cores in the virtual machine (m), a period for the virtual machine with m cores, and the blocking time when a virtual machine does not have access to the underlying hardware in each period.

div.head: INTRODUCTION
div.p: As virtualization emerges, the tendency is to move even real-time system with hard deadlines to a virtualized environment where a multiprocessor system is executed inside Virtual Machines (VM). However, predicting if that real-time system is schedulable or not is a challenging task. Today, all physical servers have many cores. Virtualization makes it possible to run multiple VMs on one physical server. It is possible to configure the VMs such that each VM uses all or a subset of the physical cores. Many VMs may, however, time share the same set of physical cores.

VMs are managed by a hypervisor. In order to be costeffective and benefit from other advantages with virtualization also for real-time systems, one would like to run periodic realtime tasks with hard deadlines inside VMs. In order to guarantee real-time properties for the tasks inside the VM we need to be able to guarantee that the VM is executed at least a certain amount of time during a specified time period, i.e., we must provide a period and a minimum execution time within that period for the VM running the real-time tasks. This has been studied for VMs with one core [1]. The problem of guaranteeing real-time properties becomes much more complex if the task set is executed on a multiprocessor [2], and running the task set in a VM with many cores adds additional complexity compared to the unvirtualized multiprocessor case. In this paper we have developed a utilization-based schedulability test for a task set running in a VM with m virtual cores. In order to avoid Dhall's effect (to be explained later) we classify tasks into two priority classes, light tasks and heavy tasks (this is the state-of-the-arttechnique for avoiding Dhall's effect).

The CPU utilization U, is the fraction of processor time spent executing a task set Ȟ ൌ ሼ߬ ଵ ǡ ǥ ǡ ߬ ሽ. U is calculated by summing up the contribution of each task ߬ ‫ݑ(‬ ൌ ‫ܥ‬ ܶ Τ ) [3]; ‫ܥ‬ is the worst case computation time for ߬ and ܶ is the period of ߬ . In this paper we propose an algorithm that provides a utilization-based test that shows if a task set is schedulable or not. If the task set is schedulable the algorithm provides the priority for each task. The input to the algorithm is the task set Ȟ, the number of cores in the virtual machine (m), a period for the virtual machine with m cores, and the blocking time during each period when the virtual machine does not have access to the underlying hardware.

The rest of this paper is the following, Section two contains background and related work, Section three provides the problem definition, Section four describes the proposed algorithm, Section five gives a concrete example, and finally, Section six draws conclusions.

div.head: II. BACKGROUND AND RELATED WORK
div.p: Liu and Layland have shown that for uni-processors rate monotonic (RM) priority assignment is optimal among all fixedpriority schemes since no other fixed-priority scheme can schedule a task set that cannot be scheduled by RM [4]. They derived an upper bound of system utilization for a uni-processor scheduling for a task set of n tasks see (3).

This bound tends to 69% for an infinitely large task sets. This bound is, however, limited to uniprocessor systems. There are two approaches to extend preemptive tasks model to multiprocessor systems, partitioned and global scheduling. In the partitioned approach, a task is statically allocated to a particular processor. i.e., a task is not allowed to migrate to another processor.

In the global approach, any tasks can execute on any processor. At every moment the m highest priority tasks among the tasks that have arrived but not finished their execution are selected for execution on the m processors using preemption and migration if necessary. This is the most common way to schedule non real-time tasks on multiprocessor systems, and it is in many cases practical to handle non real-time and real-time tasks in a uniform manner.

The theory behind uniprocessor scheduling can be used for partitioned multiprocessor scheduling, e.g., the well-known uniprocessor schedulability test [5]. However, when it comes to global scheduling, the so called Dhall's effect shows that a direct application of the RM priority assignment scheme may result in failure to meet deadlines even for systems with very low multiprocessor utilization regardless of how many processors are used [6]. In Fig. 1 eight tasks run on a multiprocessor with seven processor (m = 7), Dhall's effect occurs if we assign priorities based on task's period without considering task's utilization, for instance ߬ ଼ misses its deadline even though the system utilization ܷܵ ൌ ൫ሺ ‫כ‬ ʹ ͳͲ Τ ሻ ͻ ͳͳ Τ ൯Ȁ ൌ ͲǤ͵ͳ. Even if we reduce ‫ܥ‬ ሺ݅ ൌ ͳǡ ǥ ǡሻ to 1 and increase ‫ܥ‬ ଼ to 10, ߬ ଼ will still miss the deadline, even though ܷܵ ൌ ൫ሺ ‫כ‬ ͳ ͳͲ Τ ሻ ͳͲ ͳͳ Τ ൯Ȁ ൌ ͲǤʹ͵Ͳ.

Dhall's effect does not occur for liquid task sets [7]; in liquid task set each task has a very small utilization. If we consider any arbitrary task set, Dhall's effect can be avoided by dividing the tasks into two priority classes based on task utilization, namely heavy and light. The heavy tasks, i.e., the tasks with high utilization, get higher priority than the light tasks. In [8], the authors came up with a utilization bound of 33% for an infinitely large number of processors when using the heavy/light classification. Later on an optimal bound of 37,5 % was derived by Lundberg in [2]. In virtualized systems it is not possible to define a schedulability bound based on a fixed (multiprocessor) utilization. The reason for this is that even systems with very low utilization may miss deadlines if the period of the task is shorter than the length of the time interval that the virtual processor does not have access to the physical hardware.

In [9], the authors studied a reservation-based algorithm, i.e., a constant bandwidth server (CBS) on top of Earliest Deadline First (EDF) for scheduling real-time tasks with hard deadlines on VMs. A reservation-based scheduler allocates a computation budget for every reservation period to each VM. The execution of a VM does not depend on the other VMs running on the same hardware (temporal isolation), rather it depends only on task's period and execution time. The results show that VM technology and scheduling algorithm can affect the real-time application performance. They propose to use less pessimistic analysis to dimension the VM scheduling parameters if one uses CBS algorithm.

In [10], the authors developed a Compositional Scheduling Architecture (CSA) that is built on the Xen virtualization platform. The architecture allows timing isolation among virtual machines and supports timing guarantees for real-time tasks running on each virtual machine. The study uses pessimistic approach where every VMs is treated in isolation. In [11], the authors present a model that includes the cache related in hierarchical scheduling while keeping temporal isolation between applications that share a single processor.

In [12], the author proposes a mechanism to schedule soft real-time systems, which provide a temporal isolation between VMs that share a CPU. In [13], [14], the authors present a model that accounts for the overhead, in compositional hierarchical scheduling for uniprocessor. In [15] Compositional scheduling theory was also applied for multi-core VM scheduler for Xen real-time virtualization platform.

In connection with hard deadlines systems, the utilization has been studied for real-time systems that respond to external environment within a specific deadline that is called age constraint. This age constraint is the time between the beginning of the execution of a task in one period and the end of the task in the next period [16]. In this paper we use ideas from the age constraint approach for scheduling real-time tasks in the VMs.

In [1], the authors addressed the problem of scheduling hard real-time applications in a VM. The authors proposed a technique such that real-time applications could meet their deadlines when they are scheduled on a single VM. The authors considered a uniprocessor VM.

In [17], the authors gave a utilization bound of 0.35425 for aperiodic tasks where the utilization threshold is based on the maximum synthetic utilization. If the load on the multiprocessor server stays below 0.35425, the server guarantees the schedulability of all tasks. This bound was derived from the function ‫ݑ‬ሺ‫ݔ‬ሻ ൌ ʹሺͳ െ ‫ݔ‬ሻ ሺʹ ξʹ ‫ݔʹ‬ Τ ሻ the variable x is the utilization of the task with the longest period.

In this study, we propose an algorithm that provides a utilization based test. The test classifies tasks into two priority classes, namely heavy and light tasks. Heavy tasks have higher priority than light tasks. The algorithm checks each task in the task set in order to make sure that a whole task set is schedulable.

div.head: III. PROBLEM DEFINITION
div.p: We consider the problem of scheduling a set Ȟ ൌ ሼ߬ ଵ ǡ ߬ ଶ ǡ ߬ ଷ ǡ ǥ ǡ ߬ ሽ of n independent, periodically-arriving realtime tasks on m identical virtual processors in a VM that runs periodically every ܶ ெ time interval with a blocking time of ‫ܤ‬ during which the VM does not have access on the hardware during time interval ܶ ெ . An example of a periodic multiprocessor VM is Xen [18]. The multiprocessor VM schedules the arrived tasks by arranging them in a single queue and dequeues them in priority order as soon as a processor becomes available. We assume preemptive scheduling, i.e., a lower priority task may be preempted when a higher priority task becomes runnable. The preempted task is in that case put back into the queue, and the task can later be restarted on any available processor in the system. We assume that there is no overhead or other penalty for switching from one task to another. Each task can execute on at most one processor at a time.
The problem is thus defined by four parameters:

div.p: Based on these four parameters we want to determine: • If we can guarantee that Ȟ ൌ ሼ߬ ଵ ǡ ߬ ଶ ǡ ߬ ଷ ǡ ǥ ǡ ߬ ሽ is schedulable using m virtual processors, a blocking time ‫ܤ‬ and a period ܶ ெ for the VM. • In case we can guarantee that Ȟ is schedulable, how should we assign priorities to the n tasks.

Tasks can be either heavy or light (based on their utilization). Heavy tasks get higher priority than light tasks, and light tasks get priorities according to the Rate Monotonic (RM) priority assignment algorithm. RM assigns priorities to tasks according to their periods; tasks with shorter periods get higher priorities.

div.p: However, it is schedulable when we use the heavy and light classification (see Fig. 9).

In fig. 9, the heavy task ߬ ଼ executes uninterruptedly, as if it had a processor of its own. After ߬ ଼ completes, the processor is available for light tasks. In the worst case scenario the processor P 1 will be taken by the heavy task for the entire running time, therefore there will be no room for light tasks on P 1 . By being pessimistic this is referred as decrementing the processor and remove it from the total number of available processors (see steps 4 and 9 in algorithm description in the section 4).

div.head: VI. CONCLUSIONS
div.p: The contribution of this paper is an algorithm that determines if a task set that executes in a VM with ݉ virtual cores is schedulable or not. The test of a task ߬ is based on the utilization of higher priority tasks (ܷԢԢ). Based on the period of the VM (ܶ ெ ) and the time that the VM is blocked in each period ‫,)ܤ(‬ we calculate the parameters T, a, b, c, and z. If the task set is schedulable, our algorithm provides a priority assignment list for the tasks in the real-time system, i.e., during the test we determine which tasks should be heavy and which should be light.
